entries.name: Roman legionary fortress (castrum)
entries.purpose: legionary base and frontier control point; a town-sized planned settlement that outlived the army that built it
parts: rounded-corner rectangle on a strict grid
via principalis and via praetoria crossing at the centre
layout: about 450 x 400 m inside the rampart, one legion per fortress
streets cross at right angles; headquarters at the crossing
barracks in identical rows along the grid
rampart and ditch all round, gates on the four axes
entries.found: on the frontiers (Rhine-Danube limes, Hadrian's Wall, Syria) and in conquered provinces; many survive as city cores (Chester, York, Cologne, Vienna)
entries.notes: The most copied plan in the ancient world: same stamp everywhere, so one blueprint serves the whole empire. Watch for chester/caster place-name endings to reuse.

entries.name: Iron Age hillfort (e.g. Maiden Castle)
entries.purpose: fortified tribal stronghold: cattle corral, refuge and court of a chiefdom, not a castle
parts: concentric ramparts and ditches following the contours
hut circles and storage pits inside
layout: contour-following rings dug into a hilltop
single narrowed entrance with massive outworks
bank-ditch-bank relief that can exceed 15 m in total
living quarters inside the innermost ring
entries.found: hilltops across temperate Europe; Britain alone has over 2000, the great ones in Wessex (Maiden Castle, Danebury, Cadbury)
entries.notes: Maiden Castle's ramparts run about 6.4 km continuously; attackers climbing fresh banks under slung stones made even small garrisons hard to take.

entries.name: Motte-and-bailey castle
entries.purpose: first-generation feudal castle: cheap, fast to raise, the control point of a newly conquered district
parts: adjacent yard (bailey) with hall and stores
wooden keep or tower on the motte
ditch and palisade enclosing the bailey
layout: motte on one side, kidney-shaped bailey against it
single gate into the bailey; motte ditch with no bridge is death
keep commands the bailey; the bailey shelters herds and hall
entries.found: Normandy, England and Wales after 1066, Ireland, Denmark, the Holy Roman Empire; everywhere fresh conquest needed a roof in weeks
entries.notes: Most are now grass humps with a ring ditch, invisible until you read the landform; weak against fire, so many were swapped for stone keeps within two generations.

entries.name: Stone keep (donjon) castle
entries.purpose: permanent seat of a lord; the real fight is meant to happen inside the keep itself
parts: great hall on the first or second floor
mural stair within the wall thickness
layout: keep on the highest or most defensible point of a small walled yard
great hall and chapel inside the keep, above the vault
wall-walk with corner towers; gate the single weak point
entries.found: England and Wales (the Norman wave), Normandy, Brittany, Sicily; the model spread to the Crusader states
entries.notes: The keep alone is the architecture: opaque, rectangular, almost windowless at ground level. If the curtain falls, the keep keeps fighting.

entries.name: Concentric castle (Krak des Chevaliers)
entries.purpose: the summit of passive stone-age defence thinking: two shells, no dead ground, sieges expected to fail
parts: outer enceinte with round projecting towers, about 9 m high
inner ward behind a steep glacis, square towers
chapel, great hall, cistern (moat kept the water)
layout: ring within a ring; attackers must beat two circuits, each watched by the other
outer gate feeds a dogleg passage past murder holes
glacis under the inner wall denies siege engines a standing base
entries.found: the Crusader Levant (Krak des Chevaliers, Margat) and Wales (Caerphilly, Harlech, Beaumaris)
entries.notes: Krak held the Homs Gap for 130 years and fell only to a forged surrender letter in 1271; the outer wall doomed any attacker to be beaten from both flanks.

entries.name: Walled town with gates
entries.purpose: customs-and-taxes boundary first, refuge second; the gate is a toll plaza with a killing floor above
layout: irregular ring following the older street plan
gates at the road ends; wall-walk links tower to tower
barbican and turnpike before the gate doors
entries.found: everywhere settled wealth met stone; from Jericho's earliest wall to medieval Europe and Ming county seats
entries.notes: Footprint varies enormously: a market-town wall may be 300 m across, a walled capital 5 km. Wall-walks and gates are the reusable bits; scale the ring to the town.

entries.name: Aurelian Walls (Rome)
entries.purpose: emergency ring around Rome itself; a deterrent, never tested in a real siege
parts: 19 km brick-faced concrete circuit, 3.5 m thick
square brick-faced tower every 29.6 m (100 Roman feet)
pre-existing monuments reused as towers (Pyramid of Cestius)
layout: footprint is thickness by full length; the circuit enclosed the seven hills and Campus Martius
one tower every 100 Roman feet, alternating regular rhythm so the whole wall is overlooked
height doubled to about 16 m under Maxentius and Honorius
entries.found: Rome, Italy; large sections still stand, notably near Termini and Porta San Sebastiano
entries.notes: Raised in five years by emergency levy, cannibalising earlier buildings such as the Pyramid of Cestius. For linear walls, read footprint_m as wall depth x total length.

entries.name: Theodosian Walls (Constantinople)
entries.purpose: the definitive triple city wall of late antiquity; proof that layered depth beats single mass
parts: moat (fossa) about 20 m wide and 7 m deep
inner wall about 12 m with 96 towers
floodgates at the Marmara and Golden Horn ends
layout: footprint is inner-wall thickness by full 6.5 km length
three lines in series: ditch, low wall, high wall with towers
every 55 m a tower covers the curtain between towers
entries.found: Istanbul, Turkey; breaches beaten off for a thousand years, famously alone in 1422 and taken only by gunpowder cannon in 1453
entries.notes: Layered depth is the whole lesson: the moat stops, the outer wall absorbs, the inner wall kills. First wall in history designed against cannon and earthquake together.

entries.name: Hadrian's Wall
entries.purpose: frontier management, not a battle line: a customs border with garrisons and observation
parts: ditch to the north, vallum (earthen rampart) to the south
layout: footprint is thickness by 117 km full length, coast to coast
east half stone on whinstone ridge, west half turf on the lowlands
milecastle every 1.48 km with two observation turrets between
entries.found: northern England, Solway Firth to Wallsend on the Tyne; best preserved on the whinstone ridge east of Housesteads
entries.notes: Built in about six years. The vallum south of the wall proves the real target was controlled movement, not an unstoppable Germanic horde; gates doubled as customs posts.

entries.name: Great Wall of China
entries.purpose: a cordon of barriers and beacon chains against steppe nomads; politics and logistics, not an impassable wall
parts: cavity stone base with brick facing (Ming)
beacon towers every 1-2 km with smoke-or-fire codes
layout: footprint is wall depth by total length of the whole wall system, about 21,000 km including branches and earlier lines
rides ridge lines so defenders look down; towers sighted on each other
signal codes relay a frontier alarm across the whole front in hours
entries.found: northern China along the steppe frontier; the Ming wall is the familiar brick ridge, the earlier lines are rammed earth and often half-buried
entries.notes: No army ever 'took' the wall and none needed to flank it; the point was slowing raiders so mobile armies could catch them. Beacon-towers with smoke codes are the most reusable voxel motif here.

entries.name: Viking ringfort (Trelleborg)
entries.purpose: royal army camp of King Harald Bluetooth; rapid mobilisation and control of the Danish interior
parts: perfectly circular earthen rampart, about 137 m across
four gates exactly at the cardinal points
two crossing streets through the centre
four identical barrack-blocks in the quadrants
layout: one perfect circle, axially symmetrical
walls 5-6 m, a rampart you walk, not a masonry wall
barracks in four equal quadrants for one regiment each
entries.found: Denmark (Trelleborg, Aggersborg, Fyrkat, Nonnebakken) and southern Sweden; only a handful known, all near royal power centres
entries.notes: Geometrically exact to within a cubit across multiple sites; Aggersborg is the largest at about 240 m. Building these exact circles is a strong set-piece for a raid scenario.

entries.name: Alfred's burh (fortified market town)
entries.purpose: a network of fortified towns for a whole kingdom; defence by density, not by any single wall
parts: earthen rampart with timber breastwork, about 4-5 m high
chain of ~33 linked burhs within a day's march
layout: rectilinear grid inside a rammed bank ring
gates at road ends with towers (burh-geat)
every burh within a day's march of the next; the network is the wall
entries.found: Wessex and Mercia, listed in the Burghal Hidage; Oxford, Winchester, Chester and London all began as burhs
entries.notes: Contained the Viking advance without a single pitched battle. Footprint varies wildly (Oxford ~1 km across, Winchester larger); treat the rampart ring, not the grid, as the signature.

entries.name: Trace italienne (star fort)
entries.purpose: gunpowder-era answer to cannon: kill the attacker in the ditch with flanking fire from low bastions
parts: low sloped walls with no vertical face to shatter
covered way and glacis outside the ditch
water or mud-filled ditch, bastion angles at 90-100 degrees
layout: radial symmetry; every wall is flanked by another wall's guns
glacis slopes down so attackers are seen at maximum range
entrance across the ditch via a bridge to the ravelin, then a gate
entries.found: the Po plain (Palmanova, founded 1593), Malta (Valletta's bastions), the Low Countries, and Vauban's French sites like Neuf-Brisach
entries.notes: The plan is a fire-control diagram, not a building. Perfectly regular pentagons and nonagons for the top-down voxel view; the ditch shape is the whole silhouette.

entries.name: Martello tower
entries.purpose: single-gun coastal stopper against landing craft; named after a tower at Mortella, Corsica that resisted two British warships in 1794
parts: round stone tower with battered (sloped) base
flat roof platform for one heavy cannon
first-floor entrance reached by ladder, removable in siege
internal floors with a circular stair
layout: solitary round drum on the invasion corridor, line-of-sight to the next tower
gun on the roof; living space below; door thirty feet up
blueprint: layer 0: . . r r r . .|. r r r r r .|r r r . r r r|r r . r . r r|r r . . . r r|r r . r . r r|r r r . r r r|. r r r r r .|. . r r r . .
legend: r stone wall, . air; round tower, door at first-floor level facing inland
entries.found: the south and east coasts of England (74 towers in four chains), Ireland, Minorca, Canada and South Africa
entries.notes: Never intended to win a siege, only to smash the first boat to beach. One gun, one garrison, no surrender: a perfect single-chunk coastal encounter.

entries.name: Scottish tower house
materials: rubble stone with ashlar corner quoins
entries.purpose: defended residence of a border or highland laird; refuge, store and prestige block in one
parts: vaulted ground floor as strongroom and larder
great hall on the first upper floor
mural stairs hidden in the wall
garrets and corbelled wall-head with a parapet
barmkin (outer yard) for cattle and clansmen
layout: one vertical stack on a rocky knoll; ground floor windowless
entry at first-floor level by ladder or stair
barmkin ring outside where people shelter with beasts
entries.found: the Scottish borders and Highlands; thousands built, hundreds standing (Smailholm, Neidpath, Claypotts)
entries.notes: The basic unit of Highland land-holding; often the only roofed stone building for miles. The barmkin wall is the defensible edge, the tower the symbol.

entries.name: Japanese castle (Himeji type)
materials: tile roofs with onigawara ridge tiles
entries.purpose: seat of a daimyo and the ultimate statement of his wealth; defence through maze and intimidation
parts: white tenshu (keep) of 3-5 storeys with curved roofs
spiral bailey system funnelling to deadly choke points
layout: approach maze: outer bailey (honmaru approach), middle bailey, inner citadel
white walls blind the attacker; the true tower height is hidden until the last gate
final court beneath the keep with no retreat except downhill
entries.found: Himeji (the finest surviving), Matsumoto, Inuyama; many reconstructed after 1868
entries.notes: Himeji's main keep stands about 46 m including its stone base; 83 buildings survive. The maze of gates, not the keep, is the defensive engine.

entries.name: Rajput hill fort (Chittorgarh)
entries.purpose: fortified royal seat on a plateau; water storage for year-long sieges was the first engineering task
parts: wall circuits following the plateau rim
stepwells and reservoirs (Padmini palace pool, Gaumukh)
layout: plateau top ringed by wall; approach along a single winding road
water stored in dozens of tanks inside the walls, enough for a year
seven successive gateways (pol) in series, each with its own guard
entries.found: Rajasthan: Chittorgarh (280 ha, ~13 km of walls), Kumbhalgarh (wall 36 km), Amber, Jaisalmer
entries.notes: Kumbhalgarh is often called the Great Wall of India. Design priority: water first, walls second, palaces only after both are solved.

entries.name: Hwaseong Fortress (Suwon)
entries.purpose: royal capital-in-waiting of King Jeongjo; experiment in paid labour, gunpowder artillery and document-driven construction
parts: 5.74 km wall, 4-6 m high with 1.2 m parapets
four main gates with ongseong (semicircular gate screens)
two floodgates (Hwahongmun, Namsumun) over the Suwoncheon
gun towers, crossbow platforms, secret sally ports
beacon tower with five chimney levels
layout: footprint is wall depth by length; a near-rectangle with a spur up Mount Paldal
gates have ongseong screens so besiegers cannot aim at the gate straight on
floodgates double as artillery positions over the stream
entries.found: Suwon, South Korea; UNESCO World Heritage 1997, restored almost exactly from the 1801 construction manual (Uigwe)
entries.notes: Built in 2.5 years by paid workers, not forced labour, with pulleys and cranes — the first fully scientific Joseon fortress. Survives because the building manual survived.

entries.name: Dzong (Tibetan fortress-monastery)
entries.purpose: seat of both civil and monastic administration: tax office, army headquarters and monastery in one
parts: tall battered (inward-sloping) white walls, windowless at base
huge timber gate in an archedaed deep gateway
rows of monk cells and offices around the yard
flat roofs with monastic quarters above
often sited on a defensible spur above the river
layout: inward-sloping walls 10-25 m high, blind at the base
gate corridor bends to break a charge
single central courtyard; administration on one side, temple on the other
entries.found: Bhutan (Punakha, Tashichho, Paro) and Tibet (Gyantse, Shigatse, Lhasa's Potala is a related form)
entries.notes: A fortress that stores grain, collects taxes and houses monks. The battered white wall is so characteristic it reads instantly against any mountain.

entries.name: Sacsayhuamán (Inca fortress)
entries.purpose: royal citadel and parade ground above Cusco; ceremonial stage and last redoubt before the city
parts: individual stones up to 200 tonnes, fitted without mortar
great plaza for 10,000 troops and rituals
fine-cut stone corner joints without mortar
layout: zigzag wall climbs the hillside in three steps, flanking any attacker
the plaza above the walls could hold an army drawn up
roads to Cusco run through the fortress; it is also a gate
entries.found: overlooking Cusco, Peru; the Spanish dismantled the towers for Cusco's churches in the 1530s
entries.notes: Polygonal blocks up to five metres high lock by exact fit; earthquakes shake them, not loose stones apart. Voxel-friendly: every wall is a jigsaw puzzle of fitted polygons.

entries.name: Angkor Thom (Khmer fortified capital)
entries.purpose: capital of the Khmer Empire; royal residence, temple city and treasury in one fortified precinct
parts: 3 x 3 km laterite wall, about 8 m high
five monumental gates with four-faced towers
54 devas and 54 asuras flanking the gate causeways
royal palace and terraces (Elephants, Leper King)
layout: 3 km square grid with the Bayon at the crossing
five gates cardinal and one at the Victory Gate east
moat reflects the wall; the causeways pass between devas and asuras
entries.found: Angkor, Cambodia; the walls still stand largely intact, gate faces famously eroded
entries.notes: The giant faces are Jayavarman VII's own, four per gate, staring down every approach. The moat is a defensive moat and a reservoir at once.

entries.name: Alcazaba (Moorish citadel)
entries.purpose: fortified palace of emirs and caliphs; residence, treasury, armoury and refuge of the ruling dynasty
parts: thick battered walls of rammed earth in lifts
keep (torre del homenaje) on the highest point
inner palace with gardens and cisterns
often a walled lower town (medina) attached
layout: citadel on a crest or hilltop corner overlooking the city
rammed-earth walls in alternating hard bands, visibly layered
double enclosure: outer wall for the garrison, inner for the palace
entries.found: al-Andalus: the Alhambra's Alcazaba (Granada), Antequera, Malaga, Almeria; cousins across the Maghreb
entries.notes: Rammed-earth bands (tapial) are the visual signature — layers you can literally count. The alcazaba is usually older than the adjacent palace and plainer; the palace is the addition.

entries.name: Buhen (Middle Kingdom Nubian fortress)
entries.purpose: border control below the Second Cataract: trade, copper smelting, and defence against Kush
parts: curtain walls 5 m high and 3 m thick
double rock-cut ditch up to 8 m deep
a chain of 12-16 similar forts up and down the Nile
layout: rectangular ring with bastions on the river face
drawbridge over the ditch to the main gate
whole chain of forts within sight of each other by smoke or light
entries.found: on the Second Cataract of the Nile, now drowned by Lake Nasser; excavated 1960-64 before flooding
entries.notes: The tightest small-fort design in antiquity: bastion flanking, ditch, drawbridge, all in one package. Very voxel-friendly orthogonal layout.

entries.name: Umayyad desert castle (Qasr al-Kharana)
entries.purpose: elite estate and hunting lodge on the steppe migration routes; fortress outside, palace inside
parts: twin reception halls and a mosque
central courtyard with a fountain or basin
layout: near-perfect square, gate on the most welcoming side for the camel train
towers blind; windows high and small
single courtyard, rooms off the four wings
entries.found: the Jordanian and Syrian steppe: al-Kharana, Qasr Amra (frescoed baths), Qasr Kuseir
entries.notes: They look like border patrol forts but were weekend retreats with frescoed bathhouses. Amra's ceiling paintings are the giveaway: never meant to fight anyone.

entries.name: Transylvanian fortified church
entries.purpose: village refuge and bank: grain, wine and daughters stored behind the wall when the hordes came
parts: church nave turned into the keep
thick ring wall with a wall-walk
several towers with living quarters on the walk
storage chambers grain, wine, smoked meat
covered stairs to the wall-walk from each tower
layout: church in the centre, ring wall round it, towers at intervals
one gate, barbican in front, well inside
the wall-walk is continuous for archers
entries.found: southern Transylvania (Prejmer/Tartlau has walls 12 m high, Biertan, Viscri); about 150 survive
entries.notes: At the alarm bell the whole village fits inside with its herds; the church is where you hold out until help comes. A pocket fortress dressed as a church.

entries.name: Third System coastal fort (Fort Sumter)
entries.purpose: seacoast defence against naval attack; the US 'Third System' of masonry forts, begun after the War of 1812
parts: pentagonal brick fort with three tiers of guns planned
barbette walls on the roof platform
island site to command a harbour mouth
layout: pentagon with five fronts, each flanked by the adjacent ones
casemates on the ground floor, guns above, all facing seaward
Sumter was only partially finished and half-destroyed by its own side's guns in 1861
entries.found: the US Atlantic and Gulf coasts (Fort Sumter, Fort Jefferson, Fort Adams); mostly museums now
entries.notes: Sumter's brick proved no match for rifled cannon in 1861; the attacking Confederate guns were land batteries, not ships. Endearingly and fatally obsolete by its own christening.

entries.name: Māori pā (fortified village)
entries.purpose: fortified village and store: defend cultivated land and kumara stores from raiding war-parties
parts: rows of palisades set into the terraces
fighting stages (tahora) raised above the palisade
layout: headland pā: sea on three sides, ditch and bank across the neck
terraces step down so every defender sees over the next
palisade close-set, sharpened logs, several rows
entries.found: New Zealand; thousands of sites mapped, from Auckland's volcanic cones to Taranaki headlands
entries.notes: The palisade is the message: a fence so dense no spear can thrust through it. The most voxel-legible of all earthworks.

entries.name: Ikhanda (Zulu military kraal)
entries.purpose: regimental barracks and mobilisation camp; also a defended cattle kraal of the amakhosi
parts: circular outer thorn fence, near impenetrable to cattle and man
inner ring of huts in regimental ranks
often on a spur above a river with a cliff at the back
layout: one circle; thinner on the cliff side, thick where men can approach
cattle in the middle, regiments around, command hut at the head
screen of thorn bushes so thick it cannot be seen through
blueprint: layer 0: t t t t t t t t|t . . . . . . t|t . h h h h . t|t . h . . h . t|t . h h h h . t|t . . . . . . t|t t t d d t t t
legend: t thorn-bush fence, h hut (izindlu), d gate, . yard; cattle kraal in the centre in a full ikhanda
entries.found: KwaZulu-Natal, South Africa; bases of the amabutho (regiments), e.g. at Ulundi and iSandlwana (briefly)
entries.notes: Built in days, burned in a night: the fence stopped cattle raids and channelled attackers. A static ikhanda was a parade ground; the army itself stayed mobile.

entries.name: Mycenae (Mycenaean citadel)
materials: ashlar for gates and tholos tombs
entries.purpose: royal citadel of a warrior-kingdom; palace, treasury and tomb cluster behind walls no army could breach
parts: Cyclopean walls up to 7.5 m thick
Lion Gate with a relieving triangle
Grave Circle A inside the walls
cistern stairs through the wall to a secret spring
layout: small hilltop enclosure, wall follows the contour
single Lion Gate entrance; a postern for defenders only
secret stairs to the spring keep the citadel supplied in siege
entries.found: Mycenae, Tiryns (with walls even thicker), Argos; the Argolid heartland
entries.notes: Greeks of later ages said giants built the walls, so they called them Cyclopean. The Lion Gate's carved relief triangle is Europe's oldest monumental sculpture.

entries.name: Great Zimbabwe (Great Enclosure)
materials: dhaka (stiff clay) for floors and hut walls
entries.purpose: royal capital of the Shona kingdom: gold trade hub, ritual centre and prestige monument
parts: Great Enclosure outer wall up to 11 m high
inner passage and parallel inner wall
layout: ellipse about 100 x 110 m, walls curving with the granite outcrops
narrow bent entrances to force single file
hill complex above the valley enclosure; the two are one seat of power
entries.found: near Masvingo, Zimbabwe; the largest stone structure built in precolonial sub-Saharan Africa
entries.notes: No mortar, no dressing, yet 11 m high and still standing: the geometry of stacked granite slabs is the whole engineering. A prestige monument, not a military necessity.

entries.name: World War I trench system
entries.purpose: static front against machine guns and artillery; defence by depth, zigzag and wire, not by wall
parts: front line, support line about 200 m behind, reserve line further back
zig-zag trace to limit enfilade and blast
layout: footprint is trench width by length of the Western Front, about 750 km across France and Belgium
depth in three lines; each line covers the one in front
machine-gun positions at traverses, not exposed
entries.found: the Western Front from the North Sea to Switzerland; also Gallipoli and the Eastern Front in modified form
entries.notes: The First World War was decided by 700 km of holes in the ground. Voxel model: not a wall, a trench lattice; the defence is the depth scheme.

entries.name: Concrete pillbox (WWII strongpoint)
entries.purpose: machine-gun and anti-tank nest; anchor of the Atlantic Wall and hedgerow fighting in Normandy
parts: entrance in the rear face, blind to fire arcs
sometimes sunken so only the roof and ports show
layout: one embrasure per threat axis
sited to pair up with a neighbouring pillbox's flanking fire
rear blind to field of fire; entrance from a trench or covered approach
entries.found: the Atlantic Wall (Belgium to the Pyrenees), Normandy hedgerows, the Siegfried Line, the Czech Sudetenland; thousands survive as sheds
entries.notes: The cheapest strongpoint there is, and half the anti-tank fighting of 1944. Sunken pillboxes with only ports showing are the scariest voxel encounter of the set.

entries.name: Maginot Line ouvrage
entries.purpose: permanent frontier fortress that makes the 1914-18 slaughter impossible; defence in depth against a repeat of Verdun
parts: buried combat blocks with retracting 75 mm gun turrets
layout: mostly subterranean; only the blocks and the entrance show above ground
entrance hidden in a railway tunnel; galleries to every block
interlocking field of fire from every gun along the line
entries.found: the Franco-German frontier from Switzerland to Luxembourg; breached legally not at all, bypassed entirely via the Ardennes in 1940
entries.notes: A complete underground fortress, barracks and all. It worked exactly as designed; the war simply went round it. Walkable voxel set for real spelunking.

entries.name: Dragon's teeth (anti-tank obstacle)
entries.purpose: stop tanks dead in the open so anti-tank guns can kill them cheaply
parts: pyramidal concrete blocks in staggered rows
several rows deep, like a cable of studs
often backed by a ditch and wire
layout: staggered checkerboard so no straight lane exists
usually three rows deep, backed by a continuous ditch to block even float bridges
reserved for armour-dense approaches: railways, roads, ridge passes
entries.found: the Siegfried Line (Westwall, ~630 km), Atlantic Wall, Czech border fortifications, Albania
entries.notes: Cheap to cast, impossible to tow away in a hurry; a belt of teeth is a wall a tank cannot crawl through under fire.

entries.name: Roman limes watchtower (burgus)
materials: timber for upper storeys on earlier towers
entries.purpose: frontier observation and beacon relay; tripwire for the limes, not a standalone fort
layout: towers in sight of each other, every few hundred metres
smoke by day, fire by night; a message crosses the frontier in minutes
tower on a ridge line, fort a day's march behind it
entries.found: the Upper German and Raetian limes (about 550 km across southern Germany); the Hadrian's Wall milecastles are the same idea stone-built
entries.notes: The whole frontier thought of itself as one organism; the towers are its eyes. A chain of towers across a ridge line is the cheapest possible fortification.

entries.name: Malbork (Teutonic Order castle)
materials: carved sandstone for the chapel and gateways
entries.purpose: headquarters of the Teutonic Order: monastery, treasury, artillery depot and Prussian state capital in one
parts: three concentric wards: Outer, Middle and High Castle
Grand Master's Palace with its own defences
artillery towers and gun platforms added in the 15th c
layout: three nested wards arranged around a courtyard spine
High Castle is the innermost sanctum: chapel, chapter house, dorm
the Nogat river provides a water-filled moat naturally
entries.found: Malbork, Poland; the largest brick castle in the world and the largest castle by land area, 21 ha
entries.notes: A fortress built by monk-knights and expanded over three centuries; Red Army artillery and war damage were largely rebuilt, so Malbork is nearer 1274 than 1945.
